notes:
I've written these notes from the pages I could read. A few gaps up front: I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org, no Lutheran or Anglican source, and no page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those are left out rather than filled in from memory.

## Hebrews 4 – Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): "Therefore" carries straight on from chapter 3. Unbelief kept the Exodus generation out of Canaan. The rest is entered by faith, and it isn't enough to *almost* enter it. He passes on John Owen's five aspects of this rest: peace with God, freedom from a slavish spirit in worship, release from the burden of the Mosaic law, freedom of gospel worship, and the rest God Himself enjoys. He also quotes Adam Clarke, who hears in "come short" a picture from Greek races, where losing by any distance at all counts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown: the fear meant is not with slavish terror, but godly "fear and trembling" ( Phl 2:12 ). "His rest" means God's heavenly rest, of which Canaan is the type. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Hbr/Hbr_004.cfm
- Chrysostom (Orthodox and Catholic Church Father): links the verse to "Today if you hear His voice," adding (for Today is at every time ). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240206.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: hearing God's word is not enough; it only helps when it is "mixed with faith." That is why two people can hear the same sermon and only one benefits. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Wesley (Methodist): the word they heard did not help them, So far from it, that it increased their damnation. It is then only when it is mixed with faith, that it exerts its saving power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- Chrysostom: hearing alone did the Israelites no good. He takes "not mixed" to point to Caleb and Joshua, who kept apart from the unbelieving majority. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240206.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: "My rest" is God's own rest. He has kept it since creation was finished, and David could still speak of it long afterwards. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Precept Austin: points out the present tense: the writer does not say "when we die we shall enter," but 'We who have believed do enter.' On the oath: God swore for emphasis, not for credulity! https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_43-5
- Clarke (Methodist): Jewish believers in Christ already have the rest, a happiness in God that comes from peace of conscience and joy in the Holy Ghost. Canaan was its picture. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hebrews-4.html
- Wesley reads it differently. The psalm's rest is not God's rest after creation and not Joshua's Canaan, Therefore it is, 3. The eternal rest in heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html

**v. 4**
- Clarke: "somewhere" probably means Genesis 2:2. It refers to the setting apart of the seventh day as man's rest and a *type* of everlasting felicity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hebrews-4.html
- Guzik: the vague "in a certain place" simply reflects how hard it was to find passages in ancient scrolls before chapter and verse numbers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Precept Austin (quoted commentator): God's "rest" after creation is a picture of His settled reign, not tiredness. His reign is one of rest— that is, of absolute supremacy and unassailable sovereignty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_43-5

**v. 5**
- William MacDonald (via Precept Austin): Psalm 95's future tense shows that God's rest is not a closed matter limited to Genesis 2; God later spoke of it as still open. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_43-5
- Wesley: the psalm speaks of a rest yet to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: God did not create this rest for nothing. If Israel failed to enter, others will. The "Today" in David's psalm proves the promise was not used up under Joshua. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Wesley: "After so long a time" means It was above four hundred years from the time of Moses and Joshua to David. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- Chrysostom: David's later call shows that the speaker means people who are still to receive a reward. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240206.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: "Jesus" and "Joshua" are the same name. The second Joshua finishes what the first left undone, and the rest is found in a person, not just in doctrines. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Ligonier (Reformed): Israel's rest in Canaan was only a type of the rest to come (v.8). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rest-gods-people

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the Greek word suddenly changes to "sabbath-rest," a rest *with* God. He cites a Mishnah passage on "the day which is all Sabbath." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/4-9.htm
- Chrysostom: the writer says "Sabbath-keeping" on purpose, calling the kingdom of heaven by a name his readers loved. He counts three rests: the Sabbath, Canaan, and heaven, the true one. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240206.htm
- MacArthur (Baptist): the word *sabbatismos* involves an ultimate sense when we shall cease from all our works, rest completely as God did when He finished His creation. https://www.gty.org/sermons/1609/entering-into-gods-rest

**v. 10**
- Guzik: ceasing from works does not mean doing no good works. It means no longer relying on works to be made right with God. We cease from self-justifying works because the work is finished by Jesus on the cross. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_48-10
- MacLaren (Baptist), a less common reading: "he who has entered His rest" is Christ. He finished redemption as God finished creation, and His rest is still full of work: interceding and sanctifying. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/4-9.htm
- Ligonier: the future Sabbath rest will still contain work, the work of worship and service. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rest-gods-people
- Clarke: some say "ceasing from our works" means the end of this life's sufferings, but I understand it as including *both*. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hebrews-4.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik: God does not force the rest on anyone. Faith is not passive; it takes effort to keep clinging to Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Piper (Baptist, via Precept Austin): the paragraph's main point is "The main point of the paragraph: Fear unbelief." https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_411
- Chrysostom: faith alone is not enough here; there is need of a right conversation also. ("Conversation" is old English for way of life.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/hebrews/4.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: like a surgeon, God's word shows what is really wrong with us. It has life and power of its own; the preacher does not have to make it come alive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Wesley: "soul and spirit, joints and marrow" mean The inmost recesses of the mind, which the apostle beautifully and strongly expresses by this heap of figurative words. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- Ligonier (via Precept Austin): "For" ties this verse to the promise and the threat just given. We must pay heed, for God's Word is alive and active. It cannot be ignored. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_412

**v. 13**
- Wesley: "naked and opened" Plainly alluding to the sacrifices under the law which were first flayed, and then (as the Greek word literally means) cleft asunder through the neck and backbone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- Philip E. Hughes (via Precept Austin): the move from God's word in v. 12 to God's gaze in v. 13 is natural, because God is both the source and the goal of His word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_413

**v. 14**
- Guzik: no other high priest is called "great," none passed through the heavens, and none is the Son of God. Because He has ascended and serves there for us, we should hold on to what we profess. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Wesley: the Jewish high priest went through the veil once a year with sacrificial blood. Christ went once for all through the heavens with the virtue of his own blood, into the immediate presence God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- Clarke: the verse probably answers Jews who told Christians they had no temple, priest or sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hebrews-4.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik: "sympathize" means "to suffer along with." He contrasts this with the Greek idea that God feels nothing. Jesus had no sinful nature pulling at Him from inside, but He faced outside temptation more fiercely than we ever will. He quotes Spurgeon that sin hardens, so a Christ who had sinned would be *less* tender, not more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Gill (Baptist): Christ had no sin in His nature, and when Satan tempted Him he could find none in him to work upon. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/hebrews/4-15.html
- Wesley: He sympathizes even with our innocent infirmities, wants, weaknesses, miseries, dangers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html

**v. 16**
- Guzik: mercy is *not getting* what we deserve; grace is *getting* what we don't deserve. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Wesley: come Without any doubt or fear. It is a throne that grace set up, where grace rules and gives freely. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- Spurgeon (via Precept Austin): this is not a throne of justice, so even our broken, stammering prayers are welcome there. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_416
- JFB: *Mercy* especially refers to the remission and removal of sins *grace,* to the saving bestowal of spiritual gifts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/hebrews-4.html

## Where traditions differ

**vv. 1, 11 – Can a believer fall away?**
- Wesley (Methodist) says plainly that "fall" means Into perdition. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- Guzik also warns that we may fall as Israel did. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- Precept Austin aims the warning especially at those wavering in faith or merely professing without truly possessing saving faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_411
- I did not find a Reformed page arguing this point directly from Hebrews 4.

**vv. 3, 9 – Is the rest now or after death?**
- Wesley and JFB: mainly the future rest in heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-4.html
- MacLaren: we lose much by moving it all into the future. His point is that faith, not death, is the way in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/4-9.htm
- Clarke holds both. Ligonier stresses the rest still to come. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rest-gods-people

**v. 9 – Does this keep a weekly Sabbath binding?**
- JFB says yes, indirectly: This verse indirectly establishes the obligation of the Sabbath still; for the type continues until the antitype supersedes it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/hebrews-4.html
- A source quoted on Precept Austin argues the opposite: Hebrews 4 is teaching the exact opposite of the Sabbatarian position. In its view the real issue is falling away from the faith, not which day to keep. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_48-10

**v. 15 – Could Jesus have sinned?**
- Desiring God (Baptist) argues He could not. It notes the debate over whether "without sin" describes the *outcome* of His temptations or the fact that temptation had no foothold *inside* Him, and sides with Daniel Wallace's view of the second. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/could-jesus-have-sinned
- On the other side, Guzik quotes Leon Morris calling Jesus' sinlessness at least in part, an earned sinlessness as he gained victory after victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/

**v. 12 – Is a person two parts or three?**
- Leon Morris (via Precept Austin) says the verse should not be used to argue for two-part ("dichotomist") or three-part ("trichotomist") views of human nature. The point is how deep God's word reaches. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_412
- Another writer on the same page treats soul (*psuche*) and spirit (*pneuma*) as different: the soul is the physical life we share with animals, the spirit is what makes us kin to God. Same URL.

## Other views

- **Orthodox and Catholic (Chrysostom):** three rests (Sabbath, Canaan, the kingdom of heaven); "Today" means every day; and a right way of life is needed alongside faith (v. 11). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240206.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/hebrews/4.htm
- **Catholic (v. 15):** Catholic Answers says Jesus was and is sinless, cites the Catechism (CCC 467), and insists that Jesus could not have sinned at all. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/could-jesus-have-sinned-absolutely-not
- **A Protestant–Catholic contrast (v. 16):** Guzik says the devil sometimes urges believers to come to God by Mary or by the saints instead of Jesus. I did not find a Catholic page answering this from Hebrews 4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
- **Something you may want to check (vv. 2, 12):** Guzik says more expectation of blessing brings more blessing, and his list on God's word includes bringing "prosperity and success" (citing Psalm 1:3). He does not connect this to prosperity teaching, and I found no source that does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-4/
